purpose: Evidence-reviewed clinical additions and replacements for the generated UKMLA card dataset.

conditions.name: Urinary tract infection

fields.investigations: Clinical diagnosis. Do not use urine dipsticks to diagnose UTI in adults aged 65 years or over or in people with an indwelling urinary catheter. Send urine culture when indicated, including men, pregnancy, recurrent/atypical UTI, pyelonephritis, treatment failure and suspected catheter-associated UTI; obtain before antibiotics where feasible.
fields.treatment: Uncomplicated lower UTI in a non-pregnant younger woman: follow current local/NICE antimicrobial guidance, commonly nitrofurantoin if renal function is suitable. In older or catheterised adults, treat only when compatible clinical features support infection; do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.
fields.escalation: Same-day/urgent assessment for pyelonephritis or sepsis, pregnancy with systemic illness, AKI, obstruction/retention, catheter-associated systemic illness, inability to maintain oral intake or marked clinical deterioration.
fields.mimics: STI/urethritis, vaginitis, overactive bladder, interstitial cystitis, stones, bladder cancer and prostatitis; in older adults also consider pneumonia/other infection, dehydration, constipation, urinary retention, pain, medication effects and metabolic causes of delirium.
fields.redFlags: Fever or hypothermia, flank pain, rigors, vomiting, hypotension, AKI/oliguria, obstruction/retention, visible haematuria or systemic deterioration. New delirium in a frail older adult warrants urgent assessment, but delirium or bacteriuria alone does not diagnose UTI.

sourceReview: NICE NG109: Lower UTI antimicrobial prescribing
NICE NG113: Catheter-associated UTI antimicrobial prescribing
NICE QS90: UTI in adults
SAPG: UTI decision aids for people aged 65 years and over

conditions.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
conditions.newName: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS; formerly PCOS)

fields.investigations: Adults: after excluding alternatives, diagnose with 2 of 3 — ovulatory dysfunction/irregular cycles, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, or polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound or elevated AMH. If irregular cycles plus hyperandrogenism are already present, ultrasound/AMH is not required. In adolescents require both irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism; do not use ultrasound or AMH diagnostically. Assess BP/lipids and glycaemia; a 75-g OGTT is the most accurate glycaemic test.
fields.treatment: Lifestyle management and long-term metabolic risk reduction; COCP can treat irregular cycles/hirsutism if suitable. Consider metformin primarily for metabolic indications, especially in adults with BMI ≥25 kg/m²; letrozole is first-line pharmacological ovulation induction when infertility due to anovulation is the issue, usually specialist-led.
fields.escalation: Refer endocrine/gynae for rapid or severe virilisation, markedly elevated androgens, diagnostic uncertainty, infertility requiring treatment, prolonged amenorrhoea/endometrial-risk concerns or major metabolic complications.
fields.mimics: Androgen-secreting ovarian/adrenal tumour, ovarian hyperthecosis, non-classic CAH, Cushing syndrome, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease, severe insulin-resistance syndromes, hypothalamic amenorrhoea and exogenous androgens.
fields.redFlags: Rapid-onset virilisation, deepening voice/clitoromegaly, new severe androgen excess after menopause, pelvic/adrenal mass, markedly elevated testosterone, abnormal uterine bleeding or significant diabetes/metabolic disease.

sourceReview: Endocrine Society/International PCOS Network 2026: PMOS name change
2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS/PMOS
Monash Centre for Health Research and Implementation: PMOS guideline resources

conditions.name: Severe androgen excess / postmenopausal hyperandrogenism

fields.investigations: Measure testosterone, SHBG with a free-testosterone index, androstenedione, DHEAS, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, oestradiol, LH and FSH; ask specifically about exogenous testosterone exposure and screen for Cushing syndrome only when clinically indicated. Prefer/confirm significant testosterone elevation with LC-MS/MS. Testosterone >5 nmol/L warrants urgent ovarian/adrenal imaging. Predominant testosterone excess suggests an ovarian source; marked DHEAS/androstenedione elevation raises adrenal suspicion. Small ovarian androgen-secreting tumours can be occult on imaging.
fields.treatment: Treat the cause. Androgen-secreting ovarian/adrenal tumours usually require surgical assessment; postmenopausal ovarian hyperthecosis is commonly treated with bilateral oophorectomy. If ovarian surgery is declined or contraindicated, specialist GnRH suppression may reduce ovarian androgen production; spironolactone/finasteride can improve symptoms but do not remove an underlying tumour.
fields.escalation: Urgent endocrine/gynaecology assessment for rapid onset/progression, overt virilisation, testosterone >5 nmol/L or suspected neoplastic androgen excess; arrange ovarian and/or adrenal imaging according to the biochemical pattern.
fields.mimics: PMOS, ovarian hyperthecosis, androgen-secreting ovarian tumour, adrenal tumour, non-classic CAH, Cushing syndrome, severe insulin-resistance syndromes and prescribed/inadvertently transferred exogenous androgens.
fields.redFlags: New or rapidly progressive postmenopausal hirsutism, deepening voice, clitoromegaly, rapidly progressive androgenic alopecia, increased muscle mass, erythrocytosis, pelvic/adrenal mass or severe biochemical androgen excess.

sourceReview: Society for Endocrinology Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation of Androgen Excess in Women, 2025
JCEM review: Postmenopausal Hyperandrogenism
Endocrine Society/International PCOS Network PMOS resources

conditions.name: Coxsackie / enterovirus infection

fields.investigations: Typical hand-foot-and-mouth disease/herpangina is clinical: fever/sore throat, painful oral ulcers and vesicles on hands/feet; no routine tests. If severe/atypical, neonatal, CNS or cardiac features, discuss targeted enterovirus PCR.
fields.treatment: Supportive: fluids, soft/cool foods, paracetamol or ibuprofen if suitable; no antibiotics for uncomplicated viral disease and no routine antiviral treatment.
fields.escalation: Same-day/ED if dehydration, sepsis, meningism/encephalopathy, neonatal illness, immunocompromise, or suspected myocarditis/pericarditis (chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations/syncope).
fields.mimics: HSV gingivostomatitis, aphthous ulcers, chickenpox, scarlet fever, mpox, meningococcal disease; pleurodynia can mimic ACS, PE or pneumonia.
fields.redFlags: Unable to maintain fluids/low urine, altered consciousness or meningism, rapidly worsening systemic illness, chest pain with dyspnoea/palpitations/syncope, or a febrile/unwell neonate.

sourceReview: NHS: Hand, foot and mouth disease
Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust: Enterovirus PCR clinical indications
UK NHS enterovirus laboratory guidance

conditions.name: Costochondritis

fields.investigations: Clinical after excluding serious chest-pain causes: localised parasternal pain is reproducible by palpation and worse with movement/deep inspiration. Reproducibility supports the diagnosis but does not itself exclude ACS; investigate cardiac/pulmonary causes according to risk and presentation.
fields.treatment: Reassure, modify provoking activity and consider local heat; paracetamol. If an NSAID is suitable, Tayside first-choice ibuprofen at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time (e.g. 200–400 mg up to TDS; max 1.2 g/day OTC), assessing GI/renal/CV risk and gastroprotection need.
fields.escalation: Urgent/ED assessment if ACS, PE, aortic dissection, pneumothorax or sepsis is possible; review persistent/recurrent pain, focal swelling (Tietze syndrome), fever/systemic illness or diagnostic uncertainty.
fields.mimics: ACS, pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pneumonia/pleurisy, GORD, intercostal muscle strain, Tietze syndrome, herpes zoster.
fields.redFlags: Pressure/heaviness or exertional pain, radiation to arm/jaw/back, dyspnoea, syncope, haemoptysis, hypoxia, shock, fever/rigors, unequal pulses or rapidly worsening severe pain.

sourceReview: NHS Nottinghamshire: Costochondritis

conditions.name: Labyrinthitis / vestibular neuritis

fields.investigations: Acute continuous vertigo lasting days with nausea/gait unsteadiness; labyrinthitis has hearing loss/tinnitus, vestibular neuritis does not. HINTS is for acute vestibular syndrome only and should be performed by a trained clinician; include otoscopy and bedside hearing assessment.
fields.treatment: For severe symptoms, use a vestibular suppressant/antiemetic only briefly (usually no more than 3 days), e.g. prochlorperazine 5 mg TDS if suitable; encourage early mobilisation and vestibular rehabilitation once tolerated.
fields.escalation: Immediate stroke pathway for central signs or unexplained acute vestibular syndrome when trained HINTS is unavailable. Sudden unexplained hearing loss developing over 3 days or less and within the past 30 days requires immediate ENT/ED assessment (within 24 h).
fields.mimics: Posterior circulation stroke, BPPV, Ménière disease, vestibular migraine, acoustic neuroma, otitis media, drug toxicity.
fields.redFlags: New focal neurology, inability to walk unaided/severe truncal ataxia, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus/skew, severe new headache, or sudden unilateral hearing loss.

sourceReview: NICE NG127: Suspected neurological conditions — acute vestibular syndrome/HINTS

conditions.name: Diabetic foot ulcer / infection

fields.investigations: In any unwell or septic person with diabetes, remove shoes and socks and inspect both feet as a possible infection source. Assess ulcer depth/extent, erythema, discharge, pulses/perfusion and neuropathy; check observations, glucose/ketones, FBC/CRP and U&E. Take appropriate cultures if infected and blood cultures if septic; foot X-ray if deep infection/osteomyelitis is suspected, with MRI if uncertainty remains.
fields.treatment: For limb- or life-threatening diabetic foot disease, give acute sepsis care and antibiotics according to local diabetic-foot guidance; off-load, debride when appropriate, treat ischaemia and optimise glycaemia. Do not give antibiotics for an uninfected diabetic foot ulcer.
fields.escalation: Immediate acute-services assessment and inform the multidisciplinary foot care team for ulceration with fever/sepsis, limb ischaemia, gangrene or suspected deep soft-tissue/bone infection. Other active diabetic foot problems should be referred within 1 working day for specialist triage within a further working day; involve vascular surgery, orthopaedics and microbiology/ID as indicated.
fields.mimics: Acute Charcot arthropathy, cellulitis without ulceration, pressure injury, arterial or venous ulcer, gout, fracture/trauma and vasculitis.
fields.redFlags: Sepsis or systemic deterioration, rapidly spreading infection, critical limb ischaemia/rest pain, gangrene or necrosis, deep infection/abscess, exposed bone or rapidly progressive tissue loss.

sourceReview: NICE NG19: Diabetic foot problems — active problems, urgent referral and infection management
NICE NG19: Diabetic foot infection antimicrobial principles
NHS Tayside diabetic foot pathway teaching, 25 Sep 2026

conditions.name: Acute Charcot arthropathy

fields.investigations: Suspect acute Charcot in diabetes with a unilateral red, hot, swollen foot with or without deformity, especially with peripheral neuropathy or renal failure; pain may be absent. Arrange a weight-bearing X-ray of the affected foot and ankle; consider MRI if the X-ray is normal but suspicion remains.
fields.treatment: Keep the affected foot non-weight-bearing/off-loaded until definitive specialist treatment. The multidisciplinary foot care service usually uses a non-removable off-loading device when suitable; optimise diabetes and ongoing foot protection.
fields.escalation: Refer within 1 working day to the multidisciplinary foot care service for triage within 1 further working day. Use immediate acute pathways instead if there is sepsis, ulceration with limb ischaemia, gangrene or another limb- or life-threatening diabetic foot problem.
fields.mimics: Cellulitis, osteomyelitis, gout, DVT, septic arthritis, fracture/trauma and other causes of a hot swollen foot.
fields.redFlags: A hot swollen neuropathic foot is concerning even without pain or obvious deformity. Ulceration/infection, fever or sepsis, ischaemia/gangrene, fracture or rapidly developing deformity require urgent escalation.

sourceReview: NICE NG19: Charcot arthropathy — recognition, imaging, referral and off-loading
NHS Tayside diabetic foot pathway teaching, 25 Sep 2026

conditions.name: Infant supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)

fields.investigations: ABCDE, assess perfusion and obtain 12-lead ECG/rhythm strip. SVT is typically abrupt, fixed-rate, regular narrow-complex tachycardia, often >220/min in infants, with absent or retrograde P waves; monitor BP and SpO2.
fields.treatment: Haemodynamically stable regular narrow-complex SVT: under clinical monitoring, briefly apply an ice/cold pack to the infant's upper face to trigger the vagal diving reflex. Keep nose and mouth unobstructed; do not submerge the infant or press the eyes. Vagal stimulation temporarily slows AV-nodal conduction and may terminate AV-node-dependent re-entry. Older cooperative children: modified Valsalva.
fields.escalation: If vagal manoeuvres fail, give rapid IV adenosine with ECG monitoring, appropriate access and paediatric support. Decompensated circulatory failure: immediate synchronised cardioversion, starting at 1 J/kg and doubling up to 4 J/kg; do not delay for vagal manoeuvres. Seek paediatric cardiology advice.
fields.mimics: Sinus tachycardia due to fever, pain, dehydration or sepsis (variable rate, usually discernible sinus P waves); atrial flutter, focal atrial tachycardia and ventricular tachycardia.
fields.redFlags: Poor feeding, pallor, lethargy, irritability, diaphoresis, prolonged persistent tachycardia, hypotension, reduced consciousness, hepatomegaly/heart failure or shock.

sourceReview: Resuscitation Council UK 2025 Paediatric Life Support (basic and advanced), tachyarrhythmia section: https://www.resus.org.uk/professional-library/2025-resuscitation-guidelines/paediatric-basic-life-support-guidelines

conditions.name: Perioperative interruption and restart of antiplatelet therapy

fields.investigations: Identify indication (primary vs secondary prevention, ACS, PCI/stent date and complexity), aspirin alone vs DAPT, planned procedure and neuraxial anaesthesia; assess surgical bleeding against stent-thrombosis risk. Discuss recent PCI/ACS or DAPT with cardiology, surgery and anaesthesia.
fields.treatment: Low-bleeding-risk procedures may allow continuation; usually continue aspirin after PCI. If interruption is agreed: clopidogrel at least 5 days (UKCPA generally 7 days for elective clopidogrel monotherapy or neuraxial block); ticagrelor at least 3 days (5 before neuraxial block); prasugrel 7 days. Extremely high bleeding-risk procedures may also require stopping aspirin.
fields.escalation: Defer elective non-cardiac surgery until the recommended DAPT course is complete where feasible. Restart interrupted P2Y12 therapy as soon as haemostasis permits, preferably within 48 hours, following the agreed MDT plan. Do not routinely use heparin/LMWH to bridge antiplatelet interruption; exceptional IV bridging is cardiologist-led.
fields.mimics: Do not confuse antiplatelet interruption with DOAC/warfarin perioperative anticoagulation protocols. Aspirin primary prevention, established vascular disease, and recent coronary stents carry different thrombotic risks; minor procedures may not require treatment interruption.
fields.redFlags: Recent ACS or PCI/stent (especially within 1 month), complex PCI or previous stent thrombosis, stopping both agents in DAPT, neuraxial block before adequate P2Y12 washout, high-risk intracranial surgery, serious postoperative bleeding or new ischaemic chest pain.

sourceReview: UKCPA Handbook of Perioperative Medicines — Dual Antiplatelet Therapy: https://periop-handbook.ukclinicalpharmacy.org/drug/aspirin-as-dual-antiplatelet-therapy/
UKCPA Handbook of Perioperative Medicines — Clopidogrel: https://periop-handbook.ukclinicalpharmacy.org/drug/clopidogrel/

conditions.name: Metformin: mechanism of glucose lowering

fields.investigations: For use in type 2 diabetes, monitor HbA1c/glucose, eGFR before initiation and periodically, and vitamin B12 when symptoms or risk factors suggest deficiency. It is a biguanide, not an insulin secretagogue.
fields.treatment: Principal glucose-lowering action: suppress hepatic gluconeogenesis (and glycogenolysis), reducing endogenous glucose output. It also improves peripheral insulin sensitivity/glucose uptake and alters intestinal glucose handling. AMPK and other cellular pathways contribute; no single pathway fully explains all effects. It does not directly stimulate pancreatic insulin release.
fields.escalation: Use renal-adjusted dosing; contraindicated if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m². Temporarily withhold during significant dehydration, AKI, sepsis or hypoxic illness; suspected metformin-associated lactic acidosis requires emergency assessment and cessation.
fields.mimics: Contrast mechanisms: sulfonylureas stimulate beta-cell insulin secretion (hypoglycaemia risk); SGLT2 inhibitors increase urinary glucose excretion; GLP-1 receptor agonists enhance glucose-dependent insulin release and suppress glucagon. Metformin monotherapy rarely causes hypoglycaemia.
fields.redFlags: Persistent gastrointestinal intolerance, symptomatic B12 deficiency (neuropathy or macrocytic anaemia), severe renal impairment, vomiting/dehydration, or acidotic breathing with abdominal pain and lethargy suggesting lactic acidosis.

sourceReview: UK electronic medicines compendium (eMC), Metformin Hydrochloride 500 mg SmPC, sections 4.2-4.4 and 5.1 (updated July 2025): https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/product/13959/smpc
Rena G et al., The mechanisms of action of metformin (Diabetologia 2017): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28776086/

conditions.name: Zika virus: travel prevention and absence of a vaccine

fields.investigations: Travel and mosquito/sexual exposure history; often asymptomatic. Symptomatic Zika may cause mild fever, rash, arthralgia and conjunctivitis. Assess pregnancy status; discuss appropriate Zika testing with infection specialists/UKHSA if indicated. Urgently exclude malaria in a febrile traveller returning from a malaria-risk area.
fields.treatment: No licensed Zika vaccine, preventive drug or specific antiviral treatment. Prevention is daytime Aedes bite avoidance: 50% DEET repellent if suitable (including pregnancy; age over 2 months), covering clothing and insecticide-treated nets/screens. Symptomatic care: fluids and paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs until dengue is excluded.
fields.escalation: Pregnant travellers or those planning pregnancy need pre-travel risk discussion; during major outbreaks consider deferring non-essential travel. After possible exposure in pregnancy, seek midwife/GP assessment even if asymptomatic. For pregnancy planning, UKHSA advises protection against conception/sexual transmission for 2 months after a female traveller's last possible exposure and 3 months after male or both partners' exposure; use barriers throughout pregnancy if a partner has been exposed.
fields.mimics: Dengue, chikungunya, malaria, rubella, measles and other viral exanthems; distinguish Zika (no vaccine) from vaccine-preventable yellow fever or Japanese encephalitis.
fields.redFlags: Pregnancy with possible Zika exposure (congenital Zika syndrome/microcephaly risk), severe neurological symptoms such as ascending weakness (Guillain-Barré), dehydration or haemodynamic instability, or fever after travel to a malaria-endemic area.

sourceReview: NaTHNaC TravelHealthPro — Zika virus: https://travelhealthpro.org.uk/diseases/zika-virus

conditions.name: Travel vaccinations: indications by destination and traveller risk

fields.investigations: Pre-travel assessment: destination/region, route, season, duration, activities, accommodation, prior vaccines, age, pregnancy, immunosuppression, medication and allergies. Check NaTHNaC TravelHealthPro country recommendations and UK routine immunisation status; book ideally 4–6 weeks before departure.
fields.treatment: Update routine vaccines (e.g. MMR and tetanus/diphtheria/polio) as indicated. Offer destination/exposure-specific vaccines after risk assessment: hepatitis A, typhoid, cholera, hepatitis B, rabies, Japanese encephalitis, tick-borne encephalitis and yellow fever where appropriate. Certain vaccines/proof of vaccination may be entry requirements; confirm with destination guidance.
fields.escalation: Seek travel clinic/specialist advice for pregnancy, immunosuppression, complex medical conditions, young infants, vaccine allergies, live-vaccine precautions or yellow fever certification. Last-minute travellers still benefit from assessment; plan multi-dose schedules and advise if immunity will be incomplete.
fields.mimics: Vaccination is distinct from malaria chemoprophylaxis and mosquito-bite precautions. No vaccine is available against Zika, and many travel infections require food/water or insect-bite prevention even when other vaccines have been administered.
fields.redFlags: Live vaccines may be contraindicated in severe immunosuppression and generally avoided in pregnancy; unavoidable exposure to yellow fever requires specialist risk assessment. Unvaccinated measles exposure, travel to high-risk outbreak regions, or post-travel fever (especially malaria risk) requires prompt clinical action.

sourceReview: NHS — Travel vaccinations (reviewed 30 April 2026): https://www.nhs.uk/vaccinations/travel-vaccinations/

conditions.name: Atrial fibrillation stroke prevention: CHA2DS2-VASc and anticoagulation threshold

fields.investigations: For confirmed AF (paroxysmal, persistent or permanent) or atrial flutter, calculate CHA2DS2-VASc: C heart failure (1); H hypertension (1); A2 age ≥75 (2); D diabetes (1); S2 prior stroke/TIA/systemic embolus (2); V vascular disease (1); A age 65–74 (1); Sc female sex (1). Also assess ORBIT bleeding risk, FBC, U&E/renal function, LFTs and interactions.
fields.treatment: NICE NG196: offer a DOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban or rivaroxaban) when CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2, taking bleeding risk into account; consider a DOAC in men scoring 1. Do not anticoagulate people <65 with no risk factors other than sex (0 men, 1 women). If a DOAC is unsuitable, consider a vitamin K antagonist. Aspirin monotherapy is NOT AF stroke prophylaxis.
fields.escalation: Make a shared decision using stroke risk, ORBIT bleeding risk, comorbidities and contraindications; calculate Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance for DOAC dosing. Review risks and anticoagulant treatment at least annually, and sooner if risk changes. After cardioversion or successful ablation, do not stop anticoagulation solely because AF is no longer detectable.
fields.mimics: CHA2DS2-VASc predicts ischaemic stroke/systemic embolism, not bleeding (ORBIT). AF symptoms or ventricular rate do not determine thromboembolic risk. Mechanical prosthetic valves or moderate/severe mitral stenosis need specific anticoagulant guidance rather than routine DOAC selection.
fields.redFlags: Previous stroke/TIA, age ≥75, very recent embolic event, possible contraindication such as active major bleeding, and renal impairment affecting DOAC selection/dose. Age or falls risk alone is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation.

sourceReview: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, sections 1.2, 1.6 and 1.11: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196/chapter/recommendations
NICE NG196 AF management algorithms: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196/resources/algorithms-for-atrial-fibrillation-diagnosis-and-management-pdf-9082104877

conditions.name: CHA2DS2-VASc versus ORBIT: stroke and bleeding risk assessment

fields.investigations: Calculate both scores when considering/continuing AF anticoagulation. CHA2DS2-VASc = stroke risk; ORBIT = major bleeding risk. ORBIT: age ≥75 (1); reduced Hb/anaemia or low haematocrit (2); prior bleeding (2); eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m² (1); concomitant antiplatelet therapy (1). ORBIT 0–2 low, 3 medium, ≥4 high bleeding risk.
fields.treatment: Use CHA2DS2-VASc to guide anticoagulation decisions (NICE: offer DOAC if ≥2; consider in men if 1). Use ORBIT to communicate bleeding risk, correct modifiable risks (uncontrolled BP, antiplatelets/NSAIDs, harmful alcohol use; poor INR control on warfarin), and plan monitoring. An elevated ORBIT score is not in itself a contraindication to anticoagulation.
fields.escalation: Review anticoagulant treatment and stroke/bleeding risks at least annually or after a clinical change, bleeding event or deterioration in renal function. Severe unexplained anaemia, recurrent major bleeding or difficult combinations of antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy merit specialist review; urgent assessment for active major bleeding.
fields.mimics: Do not swap the two scores: HAS-BLED is another bleeding score, but NICE favours ORBIT for prediction of absolute major bleeding risk. Anticoagulation selection is not driven by AF rate/rhythm symptoms or a successful return to sinus rhythm alone.
fields.redFlags: Active major bleeding, intracranial haemorrhage symptoms, unexplained marked anaemia, uncontrolled severe hypertension, renal deterioration or dual antithrombotic therapy increasing bleeding risk. Do not deny anticoagulation solely for age, falls or a high ORBIT score.

sourceReview: NICE NG196, section 1.2 Assessment of stroke and bleeding risks: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196/chapter/recommendations
